title: Case interview maths without the panic
description: The arithmetic is simple; doing it out loud under pressure is not. Approach first, round smartly, sanity-check everything.
hook: If maths is the part of case interviews that worries you most, please read this first: the maths itself is rarely hard. It is percentages, growth, margins and big numbers, done out loud while someone watches. The panic comes from the watching, not the numbers. This guide gives you a calm routine and a few tricks so you can do the sums steadily and explain them as you go.
body:
In this guide

  • Say the approach before the arithmetic
  • Techniques that make it fast
  • Talk while you calculate, then sanity-check
  • Formulas you must know cold
  • A worked example
  • What to remember
  • Check yourself

Say the approach before the arithmetic

Before you touch a number, say what you're going to calculate and how: "Profit from the new line is units × contribution per unit, minus the fixed launch cost. Does that make sense?" Getting agreement first means a slip in the arithmetic costs you less, because the interviewer can see your logic was right. Accuracy still counts, so check as you go.

Techniques that make it fast

  • Percentages: build from 10% and 1%. For 17% of 340: 10% = 34, 1% = 3.4, so 7% = 23.8. Total: 34 + 23.8 = 57.8.
  • Big numbers: separate digits from zeros. 3.5M × 240: 3.5 × 24 = 84, then add back the seven zeros (six from M, one from 240) → 840,000,000 = 840M.
  • Division: cancel zeros first. 4.5B ÷ 1.5M = 4,500 ÷ 1.5 = 3,000.
  • Growth: the rule of 72. At 10% a year, something doubles in about 7 years.
  • Rounding: round to make the maths easy, but say so, and don't round away the answer (5.5B is not 5B).

Talk while you calculate, then sanity-check

Calculate out loud so the interviewer can follow, and catch slips together. After every result, check the size makes sense: "So about $1.5M a year. That's roughly 15% of their profit, which sounds plausible for a price change." Finally, say what the number means for the client. A number without a so-what is half an answer.

Formulas you must know cold

Profit, margin vs markup, contribution margin, breakeven volume, payback, ROI, CAGR and a simple perpetuity value come up again and again. The Formulas page has all 20 with a test-yourself mode.

See it in action: A breakeven question, done well

Question: A snack company spends $12M to launch a bar that sells for $1.50 with a variable cost of $0.70. How many bars does it need to sell to break even?

Answer: "Breakeven is fixed cost divided by contribution per unit. Contribution is $1.50 minus $0.70, so 80 cents. $12M ÷ 0.8 = 15M bars. Sanity check: 15M bars × 80 cents = $12M. ✓ So they need to sell about 15M bars in total to recover the launch cost. Next I'd want to know how many bars a year the market could take, which tells us how long payback would be."

What to remember

  • State the formula and get agreement before calculating.
  • Talk while you work; sanity-check the size of every answer.
  • Finish every calculation with what it means for the client.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer. Getting some wrong is how it sticks.

1. What is 15% of 480?

  • 62
  • 72
  • 82
Show the answer

72. 10% = 48, 5% = 24, total 72.

2. Fixed costs $3M, price $25, variable cost $10. Breakeven volume?

  • 120,000
  • 200,000
  • 300,000
Show the answer

200,000. Contribution = $15. $3M ÷ $15 = 200,000 units.

3. Cost $80, price $100. Which is true?

  • Margin 25%, markup 20%
  • Margin 20%, markup 25%
  • Both 20%
Show the answer

Margin 20%, markup 25%. Margin is on price (20/100); markup is on cost (20/80).

Try it now

A factory makes 2.4M units a year running at 75% of capacity. How many extra units could it make at 90%, and what are they worth at $3 contribution each?

Give yourself 60 seconds, out loud if you can. Speaking it, rather than thinking it, is what builds the skill.

Show a strong answer

Full capacity = 2.4M ÷ 0.75 = 3.2M. At 90% = 2.88M. Extra = 0.48M units × $3 = $1.44M a year. Sanity check: 15 percentage points of 3.2M is 0.48M. ✓
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case. This guide is lesson 5 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress.
